name: Referer header and Referrer-Policy default
plain: Tells the site which page the person came from, trimmed to the origin for cross-site links by default.
meaning: Reveals the previous site and, for same-origin or same-site hops, the full URL including query strings. Sites use it for attribution; it can leak search terms, IDs and private page paths when sites set weak policies.

web.api: HTTP Referer request header; Referrer-Policy header and <meta name=referrer>; rel=noreferrer

access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings
steps: Person clicks a link on another site
Browser applies the sender's Referrer-Policy (default strict-origin-when-cross-origin)
Destination server sees the Referer header

safari.note: Third-party referrers cut to origin by ITP

data.metric: Origin or full URL of previous page

limits.headline: Can tell a site which page you came from, trimmed to the site name cross site
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you click a link or a page loads a resource
can: Tell a site which website you came from
Send the full address for links within the same site
Include the page that loaded an image or script
cannot: Send your full page address to other sites by default, only the site name
Work if the site sets a stricter policy
See your browsing history beyond the last page
Send anything when you type an address or use a bookmark

story.what_it_is: A line the browser sends that tells a site which page you came from.

marketing.name: Referrer-Policy
marketing.pitch: Developer docs explain the header and the policy that controls how much of the previous address is shared.

story.for_you: You never see it. When you click a link, your browser tells the next site the page it came from. By default, for other sites, it shows only the site name, not the full address.
story.for_makers: Sites use it to count where traffic comes from, and to block hotlinking. It can leak search words or private page paths on weak settings. Makers set a policy to say how much to share.

use_cases.example: A blog sees which sites send readers, such as Reddit or Hacker News.
A site blocks images that other sites load straight from it, by checking the referrer.
A game portal sees which streamers or sites send players and pays a share.
An affiliate store credits a sale to the blog that sent the shopper.
An ad network uses the referrer to place an ad on the right topic page.
A news paywall treats visitors from a social link differently from search visitors.

technical_bounds: Cross-origin downgrade to origin only (strict-origin-when-cross-origin) unless the sending site sets a weaker policy
Nothing is sent from HTTPS to HTTP by default
Never sent when the previous page used no-referrer or rel=noreferrer
Path and query of the previous page are hidden by default for cross-origin links

abuse: Leaking private URLs or tokens in paths to third parties
Reading search queries from older search engine referrers

history.change: Default Referrer-Policy changed from no-referrer-when-downgrade to strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Same default adopted (trim cross-origin referrers to origin)
ITP 2.0 downgraded all cross-site request referrers to the page origin
